articles.label: City Budget
articles.headline: Pensacola's $300 Million Question: Where the City Plans to Spend Your Money Next Year
articles.dek: The city council begins budget workshops this month. A first look at the proposed FY2027 spending plan reveals priorities that will shape downtown development, police staffing, and neighborhood infrastructure.
brief: Mayor D.C. Reeves submitted a $312 million proposed budget to city council, a 4.2% increase over the current fiscal year
The plan includes funding for 18 new police positions, $14 million for stormwater improvements, and $8.5 million for downtown infrastructure tied to the Community Maritime Park expansion
Council budget workshops begin June 17 and run through July, with final adoption scheduled for September
articles.body:
The document landed on council desks last week. All 247 pages of it.

Mayor D.C. Reeves' proposed budget for fiscal year 2027 totals $312 million in spending across the city's general fund, enterprise funds, and capital projects. That's $12.6 million more than the current year—a 4.2% increase that city administrators attribute to rising personnel costs, infrastructure maintenance backlogs, and continued investment in downtown development.

Council members will spend the next seven weeks picking it apart. Budget workshops begin June 17 at City Hall, with department heads presenting line-by-line justifications for their requests. Public hearings follow in August. Final adoption is scheduled for September 12, before the new fiscal year begins October 1.

What's in the proposal tells you where city leadership wants Pensacola to go. What gets cut or amended in workshops tells you where council members think the mayor got it wrong.

Police and Fire: The Biggest Line Items

Public safety accounts for 62% of the general fund budget, same as last year. But the raw numbers are up.

The Pensacola Police Department would receive $47.3 million under the proposal, a $3.1 million increase. That covers 18 new sworn positions—12 patrol officers, four detectives, and two school resource officers—plus salary adjustments aimed at reducing turnover. Chief Tommi Lyter requested the positions in February, citing a vacancy rate that hovered near 15% through the first quarter of 2026.

"We're losing officers to Santa Rosa County and Escambia County because they're paying more," Lyter told council members during a March work session. "This budget starts to close that gap."

The fire department's allocation rises to $31.8 million, up from $29.4 million. Most of that increase funds a 3% cost-of-living adjustment for firefighters and paramedics, plus equipment replacement for Station 4 on Cervantes Street.

Downtown Gets Another Big Check

The Community Maritime Park expansion continues to drive capital spending downtown. The proposed budget includes $8.5 million for infrastructure improvements around the stadium district—water and sewer upgrades, streetscaping on Main Street, and pedestrian connections to the Commendencia Street wharf.

That money comes from the city's tax increment financing district, not the general fund. But it represents a policy choice: every TIF dollar spent downtown is a dollar that doesn't go to the city's broader tax base for another 15 years.

The budget also allocates $2.3 million for continued renovation of the Saenger Theatre, funded through the local option sales tax. City officials expect the historic venue to reopen for limited events by spring 2027, though a full performance schedule won't resume until late that year.

Council member Delarian Wiggins, whose District 7 includes several neighborhoods north of downtown, has questioned the pace of downtown investment relative to spending in residential areas.

"I'm not against the Maritime Park," Wiggins said at a May council meeting. "But when I drive through Brownsville, I see streets that haven't been repaved since I was in high school."

Stormwater: The Unsexy Priority

Flooding remains the city's most persistent infrastructure challenge. The proposed budget puts $14 million toward stormwater improvements, spread across 23 drainage projects in neighborhoods from East Hill to Perdido.

The largest single project: $4.2 million to upgrade the Bayou Texar outfall system, which backs up during heavy rains and floods streets in the East Hill and Cordova Park neighborhoods. Design work began in 2024. Construction is scheduled to start in January 2027.

Another $3.1 million goes to Carpenter's Creek improvements in the Ensley area, where a 2025 storm dropped eight inches of rain in six hours and left 40 homes with water damage.

The stormwater utility fee—currently $8.50 per month for residential customers—would increase to $9.25 under the proposal. That 75-cent hike generates roughly $1.8 million annually, according to city projections.

What's Not in the Budget

Some items requested by council members didn't make the mayor's proposal.

Council member Jennifer Brahier asked for $500,000 to study a potential city-operated broadband network. The proposal includes no funding for the study, though city spokesperson Kaycee Lagarde said the administration "remains open to discussing connectivity issues."

A request from the Pensacola Parks Conservancy for $1.2 million to begin design work on a new recreation center in the Attucks Court area also didn't make the cut. The budget does include $200,000 for a feasibility study—about one-sixth of what the conservancy sought.

And the police department's request for body camera replacements was only partially funded. Lyter asked for $1.1 million to replace the department's aging camera fleet and upgrade storage systems. The proposal includes $650,000, enough to replace cameras for patrol officers but not detectives or specialized units.

The Workshops Ahead

Budget workshops are scheduled for June 17, June 24, July 8, and July 15, all at 3 p.m. in the City Council chambers at 222 West Main Street. The sessions are open to the public but don't include time for public comment—that comes during the formal budget hearings in August.

Council members can propose amendments at any point before final adoption. In past years, those amendments have shifted hundreds of thousands of dollars between departments, added new positions, and eliminated projects the mayor considered priorities.

The proposed budget document is available on the city's website. It runs 247 pages. The executive summary is on page 12.

articles.label: Hurricane Season
articles.headline: Two Weeks Into Hurricane Season, Escambia's Evacuation Routes Remain a Mess
articles.dek: FDOT promised improvements to the 17th Avenue corridor after last year's gridlock. Local emergency managers say they're still waiting.
brief: FDOT's promised signal timing upgrades to the 17th Avenue evacuation corridor have not been completed despite a June 1 deadline
Escambia County emergency management officials say they were not consulted on the revised timeline
The corridor saw 6-hour delays during last September's Hurricane Ida evacuation
articles.body:
The traffic light at 17th Avenue and Fairfield Drive still runs its usual 90-second cycle. Same as it did last September, when Maria Santos sat in her Corolla for six hours trying to get her family to her sister's house in Montgomery.

"We left at 10 in the morning," Santos said. "We didn't get past the I-10 on-ramp until almost 4."

Two weeks into the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, the Florida Department of Transportation has not delivered on signal timing improvements it promised Escambia County officials after last year's evacuation chaos. The upgrades were supposed to be operational by June 1.

They are not.

What FDOT promised

In October 2025, following widespread criticism of the county's Hurricane Ida evacuation, FDOT District 3 Secretary David Hobbs announced a $2.3 million project to upgrade traffic signals along the 17th Avenue corridor from Garden Street to I-10. The plan included adaptive signal timing that would automatically adjust to traffic flow during emergencies and new coordination with Escambia County's emergency operations center.

"These improvements will ensure our residents can evacuate safely and efficiently when the next storm threatens our coast," Hobbs said at an October 14 press conference at the Escambia County Public Safety building.

The project timeline showed completion by May 15, 2026, with two weeks of testing before hurricane season began.

That did not happen.

Where things stand

FDOT spokesperson Jennifer Walsh confirmed in an email Friday that the signal upgrades are now expected to be completed "by late July." She attributed the delay to supply chain issues affecting the procurement of signal controllers and communication equipment.

"The department remains committed to this project and is working to expedite delivery of necessary components," Walsh wrote.

She did not respond to a follow-up question about why the delay was not publicly announced before June 1.

Eric Gilmore, Escambia County's emergency management director, said he learned about the revised timeline on May 28 — three days before hurricane season began.

"We had built our evacuation planning around having those upgrades in place," Gilmore said in an interview at his office Monday. "Finding out that late in the game, it puts us in a difficult position."

What the data showed

After Hurricane Ida prompted a mandatory evacuation of Pensacola Beach and a voluntary evacuation for flood-prone areas of Escambia County last September, post-storm analysis revealed significant bottlenecks along the 17th Avenue corridor. Traffic camera footage and GPS data showed vehicles averaging less than 3 miles per hour between Cervantes Street and the I-10 interchange during peak evacuation hours.

The county's after-action report, released in November, identified the corridor's fixed-timing signals as a primary contributor to the gridlock. The report noted that signals continued their normal cycles despite traffic volumes exceeding 400% of typical rush hour levels.

"The signals were operating as programmed," the report stated. "They were not programmed for emergency evacuation conditions."

Ida ultimately weakened and turned east before making landfall in Walton County as a Category 1 storm. No deaths or serious injuries were reported in Escambia County.

The contingency plan

Gilmore said his office has developed interim measures in case a storm threatens before FDOT completes the upgrades. Those measures include stationing Escambia County Sheriff's Office deputies at key intersections to manually direct traffic and coordinating with Pensacola Police to implement contraflow on portions of 17th Avenue.

"It's not ideal," Gilmore said. "Manual traffic control is manpower-intensive, and we'd be pulling deputies away from other evacuation support duties."

Sheriff Chip Simmons said his office can support the contingency plan but acknowledged the strain it would place on resources.

"We'll do what we need to do to keep people safe," Simmons said. "But having the technology in place would obviously be better than having my guys standing in the rain waving their arms."

Looking ahead

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has forecast an above-average Atlantic hurricane season for 2026, with 17 to 21 named storms expected. Four to seven of those storms are predicted to become major hurricanes of Category 3 or higher.

Santos, the Pensacola resident who spent six hours evacuating last year, said she's already making backup plans.

"I'm not doing that again," she said. "If another storm comes, we're leaving two days early. I don't care if it's a false alarm."

The next update from FDOT on the signal project is expected by June 30.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Brings 100,000 Visitors and a Familiar Debate
articles.dek: The July airshow pumps millions into the local economy. But residents near the base are asking the same question they ask every year: at what cost to their daily lives?
brief: The July 2026 Blue Angels Homecoming airshow is expected to draw over 100,000 visitors and generate an estimated $85 million in regional economic impact
Residents in Warrington and East Hill neighborhoods report increased noise complaints during practice weeks, with some measuring jet decibels above 115 dB
NAS Pensacola officials are testing a modified flight pattern this year aimed at reducing direct overflights of residential areas during practice sessions
articles.body:
The F/A-18 Super Hornets banked hard over Bayou Grande at 3:47 p.m. on a Tuesday in early June, close enough that Margaret Henson could see the rivets on the fuselage from her backyard in Warrington. The windows in her 1962 ranch house rattled. Her dog bolted under the bed. She checked her phone: the first practice session of the season.

"I've lived here 34 years," Henson said. "I love those pilots. I'm proud of what they do. But for three weeks in July, I can't have a phone conversation in my own kitchen."

The Blue Angels Homecoming airshow, scheduled for July 10-11 at NAS Pensacola, will mark the Navy's premier flight demonstration squadron returning to where it all started 80 years ago. Visit Pensacola projects the event will draw more than 100,000 spectators across the two-day show, with an estimated $85 million flowing into the regional economy through hotel bookings, restaurant sales and retail spending.

It is, by any measure, the biggest tourism event Pensacola hosts each year. It is also, for roughly 15,000 residents who live within three miles of the base, the loudest.

The Economics of Spectacle

Visit Pensacola's economic impact estimate comes from a methodology developed with the University of West Florida's Haas Center, tracking visitor spending surveys, hotel occupancy data and sales tax receipts from previous Homecoming weeks.

"This is our Super Bowl," said Dana Young, Visit Pensacola's president and CEO. "The national media coverage alone is worth millions in destination marketing. You can't buy that kind of exposure."

Hotels within a 20-mile radius of the base report near-total occupancy for the Homecoming weekend, with rates at premium properties exceeding $400 per night. Restaurants along Palafox Street and Pensacola Beach typically see revenue increases of 40 to 60 percent during the event week, according to data shared by the Downtown Improvement Board.

The show is free to attend. Gates open at 8 a.m. both days, with the Blue Angels demonstration beginning at 2 p.m. The Navy estimates 45,000 to 55,000 spectators per day for the main event, with additional thousands watching from boats in Pensacola Bay and beaches across the sound.

Decibels and Daily Life

Practice sessions begin three weeks before the show. The squadron flies twice daily during practice weeks—typically mid-morning and mid-afternoon—running through the full demonstration routine over the waters off NAS Pensacola.

Residents in Warrington, East Hill and parts of East Pensacola Heights sit directly beneath the flight patterns.

Tom Barnett, a retired aerospace engineer who lives on Bayshore Drive, has been measuring noise levels during Blue Angels practices since 2019 using a calibrated decibel meter. His readings during the 2025 practice season peaked at 118 decibels during a low-altitude pass—roughly equivalent to a thunderclap at close range, and well above the 85-decibel threshold where prolonged exposure can cause hearing damage.

"At 115, 118 decibels, you're not just annoyed," Barnett said. "You're covering your ears. Your whole body tenses up. And if you're a shift worker trying to sleep, or you have an infant, or you're on a work call—it's not a minor inconvenience."

NAS Pensacola's public affairs office declined to comment on specific decibel measurements but acknowledged that jet noise is "an unavoidable aspect of military aviation training."

"The Blue Angels have called Pensacola home since 1946," said Lt. Cmdr. Jessica Martinez, the base's public affairs officer. "We work hard to be good neighbors, and we're always looking for ways to minimize community impact while maintaining mission readiness."

A Modified Pattern

This year, the Navy is testing a modified flight pattern during practice sessions that shifts the squadron's approach corridor roughly half a mile south, over less populated areas near the Pensacola Bay shoreline.

The change came after meetings between base leadership and the Warrington Community Association last fall, following a petition signed by more than 400 residents requesting noise mitigation measures.

"We're not trying to shut down the Blue Angels," said Patricia Dominguez, the association's president. "We're asking for basic consideration. Move the pattern where you can. Give us accurate schedules so we can plan around it. Don't start practice runs at 8 a.m. on a Saturday."

Lt. Cmdr. Martinez confirmed that the modified pattern is being evaluated but said any permanent changes would require approval from Naval Air Forces Command and would depend on safety assessments.

"Every maneuver the Blue Angels perform is carefully choreographed with specific altitude, speed and positioning requirements," Martinez said. "We can't just move things around arbitrarily. But we're committed to exploring options."

The Longer View

The tension between military operations and residential quality of life is not new to Pensacola. The city grew up around the naval air station, which predates most of the surrounding neighborhoods. Warrington was established as a Navy town. The relationship has always been symbiotic and sometimes strained.

Escambia County property records show that homes within the 65-decibel noise contour established by the Navy—a zone where aircraft noise is considered "significant"—sell for an average of 8 to 12 percent less than comparable properties outside the contour, according to a 2023 analysis by a local appraisal firm.

But the same proximity that brings noise also brings jobs. NAS Pensacola employs more than 16,000 military personnel and 7,400 civilians, making it the largest single-site employer in Northwest Florida. The base generates an estimated $5.1 billion in annual regional economic impact, according to Navy figures.

For Henson, the Warrington resident who has learned to schedule her phone calls around practice times, the calculation is personal.

"My husband was Navy," she said. "I worked at the exchange for 22 years. This community exists because of that base. But I also think after 80 years, they could figure out how to fly those planes without rattling every window on my street."

The Blue Angels will begin their Homecoming practice schedule on June 22. NAS Pensacola maintains a practice schedule hotline at 850-452-2583 and posts updates to its official social media accounts. The modified flight pattern will be in effect for all June and July practice sessions.

Gates for the July 10-11 airshow open at 8 a.m. Admission is free. Parking is $20 per vehicle, with proceeds benefiting the Navy-Marine Corps Relief Society.
